questions.question: A sheet is folded once and a hole is punched through both layers. When unfolded, how many holes appear?
questions.rationale: One fold makes 2 layers; the punch pierces both, so 2 holes appear on opening - mirror images of each other across the crease. Hole count always equals the number of layers punched.

questions.question: A square is folded twice (each fold stacking the sheet over itself) and then punched once. The unfolded sheet will show:
questions.rationale: Two folds create 4 layers, so one punch = 4 holes, positioned by reflecting the punch across each fold line in turn. If a question mentions THREE folds, the count would be 8.

questions.question: When unfolding a punched paper, the correct order of operations is:
options: Unfold in the reverse order of folding - last fold made is first fold opened
Unfold in the same order as folding
questions.rationale: Unfolding reverses the physical history: the last fold created the innermost mirror, so it is released first. Working in the original fold order is the single most common error in this chapter.

questions.question: A paper is folded once vertically and the punch lands exactly ON the folded edge. Opening the sheet reveals:
options: One hole centred on the crease line
questions.rationale: A punch on the crease pierces both layers at the same spot; the two half-holes merge on opening into a single hole straddling the fold line. Count = 1, position = on the crease.

questions.question: A square is folded right-over-left, then bottom-over-top, and the top-left corner of the quarter-stack is punched. The unfolded sheet shows:
options: Four holes, one in each corner
Two holes on the left edge
Four holes along the top edge only
questions.rationale: Unfold the horizontal fold first: the corner hole mirrors top-bottom (2 holes, left side). Then unfold the vertical fold: both mirror left-right (4 holes - all four corners). Each fold adds its own reflection.

questions.question: In paper-cutting questions, a triangular notch cut from the FOLDED EDGE opens into:
options: A symmetric composite shape (e.g. a diamond/rhombus)
questions.rationale: The notch's mirror across the crease joins it into a doubled symmetric shape - two triangles back-to-back make a rhombus. Cuts obey the same reflection law as punches; only the shapes are richer.

questions.question: The hole-count rule for papers folded n times (each fold stacking the sheet) is:
options: Each fold doubles the layers, so a punch makes 2^n holes
Folds do not change the count
The count equals the number of folds plus one
questions.rationale: Layers double per stacking fold: 1, 2, 4, 8 for 0, 1, 2, 3 folds - 2 to the power n. Note the exception: a punch landing exactly on a crease can merge its images.

questions.question: In exam figures of folded papers, dashed lines typically represent:
questions.rationale: Standard convention: solid lines are visible edges, dashed lines are fold creases, arrows show fold direction. Reading the creases first tells you the stacking geometry before you track any punch.

questions.question: The final pattern of an unfolded punched paper must satisfy:
options: Symmetry across every fold line used
Symmetry only across the first fold
Equal holes on the left half only
questions.rationale: Every crease is a mirror the pattern must respect. An option with the right hole count but broken crease-symmetry is wrong - symmetry checking is the fastest final verification.

questions.question: A question says a paper was folded three times and then punched twice in different spots. The unfolded sheet shows at most:
questions.rationale: Three folds = 8 layers; each of the two punches prints on all 8 layers: 2 x 8 = 16 holes. 'At most' guards the crease-merging exception - punches on creases can fuse their images.
